questions.q: What is the core idea that defines GitOps?
options: Storing Kubernetes YAML files in Git instead of on a local disk, with no other change to how deployments happen
Git holds the declared desired state of the cluster, and a controller continuously reconciles the live cluster to match it
Replacing kubectl with a Git-specific command-line tool
Running all CI/CD pipelines from within GitHub Actions specifically
questions.explain: GitOps is defined by Git being the single source of truth for desired state, combined with a controller that continuously reconciles the actual cluster state to match it — not merely storing YAML in version control.

questions.q: What is the key structural difference between a push-based CI/CD pipeline and pull-based GitOps?
options: There is no real difference; both terms describe the same deployment mechanism

In push-based CI/CD an external pipeline applies changes using credentials it holds; in pull-based GitOps a controller inside the cluster watches Git and pulls changes itself, so cluster credentials never leave the cluster
Push-based pipelines cannot use Git at all
Pull-based GitOps requires manual kubectl apply for every change
questions.explain: The push model has an external system (like a CI server) holding cluster credentials and pushing changes in. The pull model inverts this: an in-cluster controller (Argo CD/Flux) initiates the pull, so credentials stay inside the cluster boundary.

questions.q: An engineer runs `kubectl edit deployment checkout` directly against production, bypassing the normal Git workflow. In a GitOps setup with `selfHeal: true`, what happens on the next reconciliation pass?
options: Nothing — GitOps only watches for new commits, not existing cluster state
The controller detects the difference between the live state and Git (drift) and automatically reverts the manual change to match what's declared in Git
The manual change is automatically committed back into the Git repository
The cluster is taken offline until an administrator intervenes
questions.explain: The reconciliation loop continuously compares live cluster state to the Git-declared state. A manual kubectl edit creates drift, and with selfHeal enabled, the controller automatically corrects it back to match Git on the next pass.

questions.q: In an Argo CD `Application` resource, what does the `destination` field specify?
options: The Git repository URL where the source manifests live
Which Helm values file to apply
Where (which cluster and namespace) the resolved manifests should be applied
The email address to notify when a sync completes
questions.explain: `source` describes where to read desired state from (repo, path, values file); `destination` describes where that resolved state should be applied — the target cluster and namespace.

questions.q: In a GitOps workflow, where does the actual approval for a production change happen?
options: When an engineer runs kubectl apply directly against the cluster
When the pull request changing the Git repo is reviewed and merged
When Argo CD's dashboard is manually refreshed
Approval is not part of the GitOps model at all
questions.explain: The PR review-and-merge step against the Git repository is the approval gate. The controller's subsequent sync to the cluster is mechanical reconciliation, not a decision point — nothing has touched the cluster until the merge happens.
